title: Changing Australia: Anika Molesworth and farming in a climate challenged world
transcript:
Speaker 0: Well, when Annika Molesworth was a teenager, the effects of the years long millennium drought were in full swing.
Speaker 0: The impacts on her family's property near Broken Hill,
Speaker 0: left a lasting impression, and Annika was inspired,
Speaker 0: to search for answers.
Speaker 0: Doctor Annika Molesworth is now a primary producer, an agroecology
Speaker 0: scientist,
Speaker 0: and co founding director
Speaker 0: of Farmers for Climate Action and joins me now. Annika, welcome to Changing Australia.
Speaker 0: Thanks so much for having me on the show. People on the land have a lot of memories of this millennium drought. What is the thing that you most remember seeing or experiencing at that time?
Speaker 1: It's true. The millennium drought struck so much of Australia that so many farmers do recall it very vividly.
Speaker 1: So I recall
Speaker 1: the days,
Speaker 1: the seasons, the years just becoming
Speaker 1: drier
Speaker 1: and hotter,
Speaker 1: and I recall vividly
Speaker 1: my first dust storm
Speaker 1: when I saw that orange
Speaker 1: rust
Speaker 1: on the horizon,
Speaker 1: and drew... It grew and it grew and it just engulfed the sky and came over our home
Speaker 1: and you couldn't see the sun anymore.
Speaker 1: And it was memories like this of the the dust storms and the droughts that really, you know, paved my way forward in looking after the environment and thinking how do we care for our natural world and the farms that rely on a healthy planet.
Speaker 0: What were you and your family doing in the millennium drought changes that you're introducing just to try and get through at that time?
Speaker 1: Well, at the start of the drought, you know, you're very unsure whether you're actually in drought at all. Yes. It's becoming drier, but you're not too sure how long this is going to last.
Speaker 1: So it was only after consecutive
Speaker 1: seasons of little to no rainfall that we, you know, removed all the livestock,
Speaker 1: but still without any rain,
Speaker 1: the vegetation was disappearing,
Speaker 1: the dams dried out, and I really saw the toll that was taking on people around me as well as the livestock and land. So the lot... You know, the birds disappeared from the trees, you know, you just... You didn't hear birds singing anymore.
Speaker 1: The
Speaker 1: kangaroos and emus, they just marched off the property and headed south towards cooler,
Speaker 1: wetter regions.
Speaker 1: And I also remember the toll it was taking on our community,
Speaker 1: you know, people were closing up shop and moving away. And you could just really feel this heavy sense of, you know, and and then the happiness and uncertainty
Speaker 1: of what was going on. And a drought is really like that. It really
Speaker 1: has a very long fingers right into the communities and all ways of life.
Speaker 0: You were travelling to the city for your education.
Speaker 0: What did you observe of city people's
Speaker 0: understanding
Speaker 0: of what was happening on the land at that time?
Speaker 1: At that time, I was really,
Speaker 1: you know, aware that there was this disconnect as in, you know, people in the city were
Speaker 1: complaining,
Speaker 1: you know, oh, it's raining. It's bad weather. You know, this term bad weather when the rain was actually falling.
Speaker 1: And my mind's eye was being cast back to our family farm, which was drying out, and you could really see the severe
Speaker 1: consequences
Speaker 1: of that drying
Speaker 1: on the property. And so I was trying to explain to my friends back in Melbourne, you know, oh, we're actually experiencing a really tough dry period at the moment and you know, rain, water is the lifeblood.
Speaker 1: That's what keeps our farms going.
Speaker 1: And that's... Yeah. It's... It really interested me, you know, the language and the stories and
Speaker 1: you know, how we explain the world and how it's operating to one another.
Speaker 0: You did your PhD in international agriculture and environmental
Speaker 0: management, which got you traveling to other parts of the world to see how farmers were dealing with climate change and other extremes.
Speaker 0: What did you learn?
Speaker 1: So I did part of my masters in Laos in Southeast Asia and then part of my PhD in Cambodia. So I spent a fair bit of time in Southeast Asia
Speaker 1: working with the local agricultural offices as well as subsistence farmers there. And we were testing and trialing different, farming practices to improve water retention in soils and productivity
Speaker 1: of the lands.
Speaker 1: But climate change was sort of this umbrella theme that I was exploring. How are farmers adapting to changes in the climate,
Speaker 1: and and what are they doing? What are they doing on the ground that is working or what is not working?
Speaker 1: And I found it just really fascinating that a lot of the farmers that I was working with who have had very little formal education in climate change
Speaker 1: were very precisely
Speaker 1: telling me, you know, the number of days the dry season is extending,
Speaker 1: the new insects that they are seeing emerging and eating their crops.
Speaker 1: They were telling me, you know, very vividly how this impacts whether their community and family is fed or not.
Speaker 1: And then I was coming back to Australia when I was doing my write up and I was still hearing in the, you know, the mainstream narrative,
Speaker 1: the science is out, you know, the the climate change debate.
Speaker 1: And I just grew increasingly frustrated
Speaker 1: that, there was this poor narrative around climate change,
Speaker 1: and the respect for science and what we learn and how we can incorporate
Speaker 1: new good knowledge to better the food and farming systems that we're operating with.
Speaker 0: In in 2014,
Speaker 0: you founded ClimateWise Agriculture,
Speaker 0: and after that, you helped to set up farmers for climate change. Why, Anika?
Speaker 1: So Farmers for Climate Action came about this opportunity where about 30 farmers got together in the Blue Mountains,
Speaker 1: and we had this conversation about how climate change is impacting us.
Speaker 1: We were from farms all over the country, different geographic regions, all different sectors,
Speaker 1: and all these farmers were sharing common stories of how, you know, it is becoming harder to earn a a livelihood if we don't do something to protect our climate because it's those climatic systems,
Speaker 1: the rainfall,
Speaker 1: the temperature,
Speaker 1: the seasons that we so heavily depend on to produce our foods and fibers.
Speaker 1: And when they shift, when we get more extreme weather events like droughts and floods and bushfires, it becomes increasingly difficult to do so.
Speaker 1: So this group, this small group of farmers decided,
Speaker 1: we're going to set up
Speaker 1: a group, a community group called Farmers for Climate Action, and let's see who jumps on board, and let's advocate for a better, a brighter farming future.
Speaker 1: And my goodness, over the last ten years, we have just had this amazing growth in people coming together from all,
Speaker 1: agricultural sectors in Australia, from urban environments to saying, we believe in this. We want a food secure future. We want a healthy planet and a healthy climate. So let's work together to help solve these problems.
Speaker 0: What's the biggest challenge that farmers are telling you about through this work?
Speaker 1: Well, climate change is a matter of urgency.
Speaker 1: It's also a matter of ambition.
Speaker 1: We need to work hard, and we need to work together now
Speaker 1: to try and solve these big complex problems.
Speaker 1: And that means we need changes in policy to make sure that we're, you know, reducing pollution as fast as possible and as responsibly as possible. We need supporting agricultural
Speaker 1: communities
Speaker 1: so they can shift from fossil fuel usage to renewable energies.
Speaker 1: So many farmers that I speak with, they would love to incorporate
Speaker 1: solar and batteries and electric vehicles on their properties.
Speaker 1: Farmers care so deeply about the environment,
Speaker 1: about these homes and places they cherish.
Speaker 1: And putting in place the best strategies now
Speaker 1: ensures that that they do have productive and profitable
Speaker 1: properties,
Speaker 1: farms
Speaker 1: that feed our country, and that they can potentially pass on to the next generation in best health possible.
Speaker 0: Farmers for Climate Action describes itself as being nonpartisan,
Speaker 0: but how do you remain apolitical
Speaker 0: when climate change is such a political issue right now?
Speaker 1: Climate change impacts
Speaker 1: everyone
Speaker 1: everywhere,
Speaker 1: and so it cannot be a political issue. It has to be something that we all work on together as a community.
Speaker 1: And so Farmers for Climate Action, we welcome conversations
Speaker 1: from people of all walks of life, so all political divisions. We want to sit down and we want to talk about how best do we ensure, you know, productive and profitable
Speaker 1: farms.
Speaker 1: How do we ensure we've got food security right across the nation?
Speaker 1: How do we set ambitious
Speaker 1: targets and put in place the steps to make them a reality?
Speaker 1: And so we welcome those conversations with with everyone across the political spectrum because we are all in this boat together.
Speaker 0: For a long time, you've been asking how to feed the world's growing population in a climate challenged world. Have you found the answers to that yet?
Speaker 1: The beauty with science and agricultural science and climate science is that we're always striving and learning, and every day we're testing and trialing. And that's what I actually love about farmers, you know, they're the ultimate scientists.
Speaker 1: Always looking at how do we improve the health of soil, the quality of our water and river systems, the biodiversity on our properties, the well-being of our livestock and,
Speaker 1: productivity of our crops.
Speaker 1: So there's never going to be a final end point. It's always going to be a push for learning,
Speaker 1: for knowing, for bettering.
Speaker 1: And there are so many ways that we can better the farming system today. We know that, you know, this is not a matter of technology or know how we know what we can do. This is a matter of ambition and determination and willpower.
Speaker 1: And when we have, you know, good strategies in place, we have good policies, supporting policies,
Speaker 1: then we can speed up this transformation
Speaker 1: to a much healthier,
Speaker 1: much more stable and productive
Speaker 1: farming system.
Speaker 0: What's your hope for the future?
Speaker 1: Well, I do think that we can have, you know, productive
Speaker 1: farming systems that produce beautiful,
Speaker 1: healthy, nutritious foods for all of Australians.
Speaker 1: I do believe that we can have a beautiful climate that we're working with, but it does mean we need to put in the hard work now that we really need to have conversations and policymakers
Speaker 1: putting in place ambitious strategies that help us get there. And we need people everywhere, whether you're on a farm or you're not
Speaker 1: championing
Speaker 1: these,
Speaker 1: you know,
Speaker 1: policies and strategies that support our environment. Because ultimately,
Speaker 1: it's not just about the environment, it's about livelihoods, it's about human health, it's about community stability.
Speaker 1: And, you know, when we do that, then we have a better and brighter future for everyone.
Speaker 0: What have the farmers that you've spoken with, what have they taught you?
Speaker 1: They have taught me so much about resilience,
Speaker 1: about determination,
Speaker 1: about fighting for things you care about.
Speaker 1: And there's not a farmer that I haven't met who cares so deeply
Speaker 1: about the land that they are nurturing at the moment. They care about, you know, the birds and the trees and the sheep in the paddock, the crops that are growing. They are getting up at sunrise every day and heading out into to the field facing the new challenge of the day.
Speaker 1: And they're doing that because they really do
Speaker 1: believe in what they're doing. And they take great great pride in producing food and fibers
Speaker 1: for all of Australians and for people overseas that we export
Speaker 1: our agricultural produce to.
Speaker 1: And so that resilience,
Speaker 1: that determination, that courage
Speaker 1: to look at challenges in the eye and believe that we can overcome them, we can work together to solve these things,
Speaker 1: like that really fills me with hope for the future.
Speaker 0: Anika Molesworth, thank you very much for joining me this morning. Thank you so much for having me. Doctor Molesworth is a a sheep, farmer and agroecology
Speaker 0: scientist and author and co founding director of Farmers for Climate Action.
themes: Climate change impacts on Australian agriculture
Sustainable farming practices and policy reform
